arxiv:2611.24738.text: Jeveration: System One Models Now Generate. From Yuhe Liu and colleagues. Jeveration tackles the challenge of generating coherent images in one fast, parallel step, where different parts of an image must fit together. It adapts a frozen vision-language model and uses a shared random state to coordinate predictions, first learning from discrete image codes so the model pays attention to that state. One model also handles image editing and dense prediction. It generates a five-hundred-and-twelve-pixel image in seventy-eight milliseconds, up to one hundred and twenty-two times faster than existing unified models, with competitive quality and prediction performance.

arxiv:2611.24154.text: Game2Player: Scaling Gameplay Experience for Visual Agents through Environment-Player Co-Development. From Xirui Jiang and colleagues. Visual agents need varied gameplay experience, but human play is expensive, and videos often omit the actions needed for learning. Game2Player creates and checks game tasks, then uses coding and vision-language players to test them and collect gameplay. It produces five hundred sixty-eight verified games and more than fifteen thousand trajectories. Training on this data raises task progress on both its own benchmark and an external game benchmark, suggesting a way to scale gameplay learning.

arxiv:2611.24789.text: HINT-WAM: Hindsight-Informed Training for World Action Models. From Phuong Tuan Dat and colleagues. Reliable robot control remains difficult because existing training methods either learn only from expert actions or rely on sparse rewards. HINT-WAM trains a model on the actions it generates itself, using future demonstration video as extra guidance for a teacher within the same model. The student never receives that future video and needs neither rewards nor simulator interaction. This approach provides dense action targets along the student's own sampling path, aiming to improve task-specific learning without sacrificing the benefits of pretrained models.

arxiv:2611.24869.text: WorldRuler: Interactive World Modeling under Configurable Rules. From Mingliang Zhai and colleagues. Customizable game worlds need to follow user-defined rules, even when those rules differ from real-world behavior and affect objects that have not appeared yet. WorldRuler stores rules, their dependencies, and object states in an executable three-dimensional graph, then uses visual feedback to guide video generation. It also links rule-defined objects to their visual appearances and trains the system to change targeted attributes without disrupting unrelated content. Tests show that it preserves rules and world states across saving and loading, and accurately depicts rule-driven changes.

arxiv:2611.24651.text: Piccolo: Co-Evolving Decision Models and Data through Recursive Self-Improvement. From Zhenqing Ling and colleagues. Building strong decision models is hard because their capabilities and training data need to improve together. Piccolo uses research agents to study model behavior, build and select data, run experiments, and feed results into later training, across models from 0.8 billion to 27 billion parameters. Piccolo-27B leads the Decision Index Vision Full leaderboard, and all three reported model sizes rank first on their respective Private benchmarks. The work also finds that carefully chosen data can help smaller models rival larger ones on specialized tasks.

arxiv:2611.24408.text: StrideWorld: Benchmarking Scene Rigidity and Action Consistency in Interactive Video World Model. From Chuang Wang and colleagues. Interactive video models must keep scenes stable as the camera moves and make repeated commands produce consistent motion. StrideWorld tests these properties using references fixed before the motion being judged, and checks that its measures match known camera motion and human ratings. Across open models, nearly all distort scenes, while many falter on routes made from several commands; only two keep most routes near the positions predicted by their own movement. Fine-tuning on a few rendered clips removes most mid-route stalls in two models.

arxiv:2611.24733.text: Mechanistic Critics for Sample-Efficient NPU Design-Space Exploration. From Yicheng He and colleagues. Exploring neural processing unit designs for large language models is costly, and simulator latency and power scores do not explain what makes a design slow. CriticNPU uses a hardware-based critic to screen weak designs before simulation and, afterward, identify whether prefill or decode is limited by computing power or memory bandwidth. Across six workloads, it matched or beat the best latency in most settings while using roughly half as many simulator calls as competing methods. This helps guide design changes with fewer expensive experiments.

arxiv:2611.24098.text: RoughCut-Bench: A Benchmark for Automatic Video Rough-Cut with Large Vision-Language Models. From Ruisi Zhao and colleagues. Automatic rough-cutting can turn raw footage into an initial edit, but it has lacked a broad way to test how well artificial intelligence systems do this. RoughCut-Bench evaluates cuts based on video content and on speech transcripts, with annotations for selecting highlights, ordering clips, and removing unwanted speech. The researchers also propose workflows that help large vision-language models produce structured edit plans. Tests show that current models still struggle to create cuts that match expert judgments.

arxiv:2611.24654.text: CurvDelta: Low-Curvature Delta Modeling For Surgical Learning and Unlearning. From Zeguan Xiao and colleagues. Adapting large language models can teach new skills or remove unwanted knowledge, but it can also damage capabilities that should remain. CurvDelta uses the model's local geometry to find update directions that keep a preservation measure nearly unchanged, with approximations that make the approach practical; a low-rank version, CurvLoRA, makes adaptation more efficient. Tests in mathematical reasoning and code generation show competitive results with better preservation of general abilities. In knowledge unlearning, the methods balance targeted forgetting and retention better than the alternatives, with retention close to retraining from scratch.

arxiv:2611.24576.text: Late Entry in Looped Language Models. From Ziqi Jin and colleagues. Looped language models improve reasoning by repeatedly applying the same layers, but each extra pass slows token generation. This work studies late entry, where new tokens skip early passes and use a deep cache of past tokens; a small fine-tuning step helps align the skipped and remaining passes. The method also lets earlier tokens finish their passes while later steps proceed, avoiding extra delays. On the tested models, it reached up to eight point four times the speed of standard greedy decoding while preserving exact outputs, and up to twelve point five times the speed when some output changes were allowed.

arxiv:2611.24830.text: A Foundation Model to Measure and Predict Human Behaviour. From Haoran Ye and colleagues. Language models can produce plausible answers about people while misrepresenting individuals and distorting population statistics. Chiron is a foundation model trained to measure psychological traits, predict individual choices, and match patterns seen across groups. Its measurements better match people's self-reports, and it predicts individual behaviour more accurately than leading language models, with gains of up to twenty-eight point four percent. In simulations of social science experiments, its estimates of human effects have substantially lower error.

arxiv:2611.24075.text: Recurrent Domain Incremental Adaptation of Time-Series Foundation Models. From Sachith Abeywickrama and colleagues. Time-series foundation models can struggle when operating conditions change, especially when only a small labeled sample is available and the condition is unknown at test time. PACT divides the model's embedding space into local regions and learns small adjustments only where a new condition shifts those regions. It keeps the original model and earlier adjustments fixed, while a learned gate chooses which adjustment to apply. With five percent labeled data per condition, it maintained average macro-F1 above zero point nine five across four bearing-fault conditions.

arxiv:2611.23751.text: Thinking Fast, Anywhere: One System-1 for the Decision Points of Any Agent Workflow. From Rui Li and colleagues. Large language model agents often spend time and money asking a large model to choose among a few familiar options. AnyS1 turns instructions in human-written skills into decision points, then uses them to train one smaller model that can make those choices across different workflows. When its confidence is low, the agent returns to the large model. On three new benchmarks, AnyS1 preserved task reliability while cutting episode costs by seventy-five to ninety-one percent and model-call time by sixty-three to ninety-two percent.

arxiv:2611.23499.text: BiCAT: Bimanual Coordination Action Tokenization. From Xuanwei Liu and colleagues. Bimanual robot policies need to represent movements shared by both arms while capturing how each arm's actions depend on the other. BiCAT uses one shared motion representation and cross-arm attention, then predicts the left arm's actions before predicting the right arm's actions based on them. Across ten simulated tasks and six real-world tasks on three robot types, it had the highest success among the compared tokenizers. In simulation, it improved mean success by 17.6 percentage points over the strongest baseline, with the largest gains on closely coordinated tasks.

arxiv:2611.24681.text: DrawScore: Evaluating Generated CAD Models against Engineering Drawings. From Haorui Chen and colleagues. Common CAD scores can miss small but important flaws, such as a misplaced hole, because the flaw affects little of a model's total surface or volume. DrawScore compares models through three engineering-style views, including visible and hidden lines, and scores differences along their projected outlines. Tests confirm that it is more sensitive to local errors, revealing flaws in generated models that standard scores judge nearly perfect. It also helps guide generation and check models against drawings without a three-dimensional reference.

arxiv:2611.23388.text: QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents. From Xingyang Li and colleagues. Choosing a low-cost quantization recipe for each language model is slow, and the best recipe can vary by model and precision. QDA uses an agent to refine recipes, with a fast evaluator that compares candidate outputs to the original model and longer generations that can reveal failures. Across four reasoning models, it beats the strongest public recipes by up to two point two percentage points on average, depending on precision. On a large model, it recovers more of the original model's accuracy than the best vendor checkpoint, with no added inference overhead.

arxiv:2611.24161.text: AVTR: Adaptive Multimodal Reasoning with Visual Imagination. From Xiaoqian Shen and colleagues. Vision-language models can miss visual details when they rely only on words, yet lengthy reasoning is unnecessary for many questions. Adaptive Visual-Textual Reasoning adds visual imagination, letting a model revisit an image and generate a reflection that highlights relevant evidence. A learned policy chooses when to use visual reflection or textual reasoning, and how to match them to each task. Across sixteen benchmarks, it raised the average score by four point five over the Qwen three point five baseline while cutting inference time by thirty-three percent.

arxiv:2611.23386.text: Chorus: Shared N-gram Embeddings with Layer-wise Adaptation. From Stephen Chung and colleagues. N-gram embedding tables can improve language models, but separate tables for every layer use substantial memory, while one shared table lacks layer-specific flexibility. Chorus shares the tables across the network and lets each layer adapt them using its current hidden state. It matches existing methods with tables that are eighty-seven percent smaller, and outperforms several alternatives across the table sizes tested. Combined with the Ember optimizer, it also cuts table-optimizer memory by ninety-nine point two percent without reducing training performance.

arxiv:2611.23808.text: PReMind: When Personal Memory Meets Visual Hazards. From Yeongtak Oh and colleagues. Visual assistants can miss the mark when a hazard in a scene needs to be judged alongside a person's allergies, health, or mobility needs. PReMind-Bench tests whether models can retrieve personal information, connect it to what they see, respond safely, and abstain when needed. The PReMind training method combines two ways of accessing memory to teach these skills together. On the interdependency test, it raises joint success from 12.9 percent to 28.6 percent over the base model.

arxiv:2611.24669.text: Movie2Game-Bench: Holistic Evaluation of Film-to-Game Adaptation Beyond Playability. From Jialing Xie and colleagues. Turning a film into a game means more than making something playable: it also means preserving the film and giving players meaningful actions. Movie2Game-Bench evaluates these goals by linking film content to gameplay steps and evidence from the game, with three model players testing each game. It covers twenty-two films and compares fourteen models, which show different strengths in game quality, adaptation, and player experience. Playable sequences are the weakest area across all models, pointing to a need to preserve gameable situations and connect film content to player choices and consequences.

arxiv:2611.24602.text: Diffusion Models are Provably Efficient Priors for Sparse Recovery. From Ivan Lee and colleagues. Sparse recovery aims to reconstruct a signal from only a few linear measurements, but strong theoretical guarantees for diffusion-based methods have been limited. This work studies a sampler guided by the measurements and an accurate diffusion model of a sparse signal prior. It proves that the sampler recovers sparse signals in polynomial time, using nearly the smallest number of measurements possible across a broad range of sensing matrices. When signals follow the assumed prior, the method also provides guarantees for sampling from the posterior.

arxiv:2611.24747.text: Cross-Vehicle Transferability of Lateral Velocity Estimation on Production Vehicles through Input Selection and Data Augmentation. From Hendrik Schäfke and colleagues. Estimating sideways vehicle speed matters for safety controls, but production vehicles cannot measure it directly. Researchers trained a neural network using signals from a compact car, then tested it without retraining on an SUV and a van. Its error on those unfamiliar vehicles was ten times higher, but choosing five signals and adding training examples that reflect vehicle symmetry and sensor bias improved transfer. Together, the two additions cut error by thirteen percent on the SUV and fifteen percent on the van, and matched a tuned model-based method on the SUV.

arxiv:2611.24857.text: Non-intrusive modal decomposition of transport-dominated data. From Robert Koprinkov and colleagues. Transport-dominated data can be hard to represent because important patterns move, and standard methods may measure their error poorly. This work develops a non-intrusive modal method that uses Wasserstein distance to judge reconstruction quality and accounts for how smoothly the modes change over time. It also allows expert knowledge to be added as inequality constraints, without requiring the correct pattern shifts to be known in advance. In tests on synthetic data and a wildland fire simulation, it reduced reconstruction error by up to forty-three percent compared with a baseline given those shifts.

arxiv:2611.24362.text: PIPETTE: Prompt Injection Purple-Teaming for Robust LLM Agents. From Lipeng He and colleagues. Indirect prompt injection can hijack language model agents through untrusted data, but finding attacks does not always help developers defend against them. PIPETTE is a framework that links attack discovery with adversarial training, using a reward that encourages a wider range of attack strategies and training agents to resist them while doing legitimate tasks. Tests on two agent benchmarks show that PIPETTE-trained agents reach near-zero success for static attacks and withstand strong adaptive attacks, while keeping benign task performance close to undefended agents.

arxiv:2611.24228.text: Functional Principal Component Analysis: Minimax Optimality from Sparse to Dense Designs and Beyond. From Shunxing Yan and colleagues. Functional principal component analysis reduces complex curves to a smaller set of patterns, but its accuracy under noisy, discrete measurements has been hard to characterize when estimating many components. This work develops a method that pools measurements across subjects and covers sampling designs from sparse to dense. It establishes optimal error rates for individual components and growing groups of components, showing how the limits shift between identifying the components and reconstructing the underlying curves. The analysis also shows that regression based on these components achieves optimal rates.

arxiv:2611.23827.text: Covering the Pauli Observables: Sampling Thresholds and the Design Effect of a Measurement Setting. From Kausthubh Chandramouli and colleagues. Measuring Pauli observables in quantum experiments can cover many observables at once, but the estimates from one setting are correlated. This work studies how random measurement settings cover observables and how that shared data affects estimation. It finds a sharp coverage threshold as the number of settings grows, and shows that random sampling is close to optimal. In six-qubit simulations, settings required seven point six to thirty-eight times fewer circuit runs than measuring the same number of observables independently.

arxiv:2611.24778.text: Counterfactual World Models: JEPAs That Reason About "What If". From Randall Balestriero and colleagues. Hidden forces can make an action look like a bad decision when it was really bad luck. This work shows that models trained only on observed outcomes cannot answer what would have happened under another action, then derives a way to estimate that outcome from the observed one and the difference between the model's predictions. It needs no extra training data or model parameters. In tests with image-based models, counterfactual accuracy rose from thirty-eight to forty-six percent to eighty-six to ninety-six percent on four simulators, helping identify actions that would have reached the goal.

arxiv:2611.24272.text: Stability-compatible kernels: beyond Gaussianity for impulse response estimation. From Gianluigi Pillonetto and colleagues. Impulse-response models need regularization that supports stable systems, but the usual Gaussian assumptions can rule out useful covariance kernels. This work defines stability-compatible kernels and shows that they allow at least one random realization with absolutely summable responses exactly when stable functions are dense in the kernel's function space. It also builds non-Gaussian priors that keep a chosen covariance while enforcing stability, including one based on the radial-basis-function kernel. Experiments show substantial estimation gains, especially for responses with late or widely separated dynamics.

arxiv:2611.24600.text: Data-driven control of polynomial systems using implicit methods. From András Sasfi and colleagues. Controlling nonlinear systems directly from measurements is difficult because methods for linear systems do not readily extend to them. This work represents the trajectories of polynomial systems through implicit polynomial relations learned from data, and gives conditions for when the measurements are sufficient. It then uses this representation for simulation and predictive control, solving the resulting problems globally with homotopy continuation. In numerical studies, it simulates a stiff Van der Pol oscillator where explicit models fail, and predicts long Duffing oscillator trajectories better than Koopman-based methods.

arxiv:2611.24333.text: A Batched Discrepancy Principle for Stochastic Landweber-Kaczmarz Iteration and its Application to EIT. From Rommel Rabongue Real and colleagues. Ill-posed inverse problems can be hard to solve, especially when they involve many equations. This work studies a stochastic method that selects a random batch of equations at each step, and proposes a stopping rule that checks the residual only for the selected batch. Under a stated condition on the equations, the method is shown to converge with exact data and with noisy data, including when stopped by the new rule. Tests in electrical impedance tomography illustrate its performance across different batch sizes.

arxiv:2611.24637.text: Hypnos: A Dual-Phase End-to-End Platform for Scalable Continual Learning at the Edge. From Guilherme Guedes and colleagues. Edge devices need to learn from changing data as it arrives, but their limited memory and power make conventional training difficult and can lead to forgetting. Hypnos splits learning into a wake phase on a small device and a sleep phase on a charger with more energy and memory. Tested on a standard continual-learning benchmark, it reached accuracy of seventy-eight point six to eighty-one point six percent. It also used twenty-two times less learning compute than quantized latent replay, with higher accuracy and comparable latency.

arxiv:2611.24662.text: Gradient-Based Defensive Poisoning Against System Identification Attacks on Cyber-Physical Systems. From Gonçalo Fernandes and colleagues. Cyber-physical systems can be covertly attacked after an attacker learns their dynamics by watching controller and plant signals. This work tests a defense that adds small, carefully chosen disturbances to the measurements the attacker sees, targeting periods that carry the most information about system behavior. In a simulated networked control system for a direct-current motor, these disturbances caused larger prediction errors than random disturbances of the same strength. They also degraded a second identification method, suggesting the defense could work in decoy environments such as honeynets.

arxiv:2611.24287.text: Parameter estimation for discretely observed rough fractional interacting particle systems. From Chiara Amorino and colleagues. Estimating drift in interacting particle systems is difficult when observations are discrete and the driving noise is rough. This work builds contrast-based estimators from observations of every particle, covering both smoother and rougher fractional Brownian noise, and also develops a method to estimate the noise parameters jointly with the drift. When the noise parameters are known, the estimates are strongly consistent and asymptotically normal. The results show that the observation-mesh convergence rate changes at a Hurst parameter of three quarters, while asymptotic normality holds in both noise regimes.

arxiv:2611.23762.text: Addressable transversal CCZ gates on almost good quantum LDPC codes and nearly optimal magic state protocols. From Shi Jie Samuel Tan and colleagues. Large collections of logical controlled-controlled-Z, or CCZ, gates are hard to perform fault-tolerantly while keeping quantum codes robust. Assuming a specific expansion property, this work builds low-density parity-check codes with nearly linear distance and many independently addressable gates that can be applied using transversal physical operations. The construction also enables magic state protocols with nearly optimal overhead: one distills CCZ states with very small overhead, while another directly prepares many encoded states at nearly linear distance.

arxiv:2611.23977.text: OMNIS+: Semantic RAN Slicing and Quantization for Dynamic Split Neural Networks. From Langtian Qin and colleagues. Edge systems need to share wireless and computing resources, but existing radio network slicing is built around fixed computing models and cannot adapt well to changing neural-network representations. OMNIS+ combines dynamic neural compression with adaptive quantization, then coordinates device choices and edge-server resources across multiple cells. Its new box quantization scheme is more resilient to transmission errors across different compression rates. Compared with leading alternatives, OMNIS+ cuts quality-of-service violation probability by up to one point seven five while improving the trade-off with inference accuracy.

arxiv:2611.24187.text: Worth Another Look:Constrained World-Model Planning for Visual Inspection. From Ziyue Kang and colleagues. Visual inspection robots must find several kinds of targets while working within tight limits on sensing and computing. This work plans which classes to query, which image regions to inspect, and when to stop, using a learned model to predict what each action may reveal and exact rules to enforce the limits. Across eight land, optical, and sonar benchmarks, looking ahead beat fixed schedules under tight budgets, improving average precision by up to twenty-eight point four percentage points on RUOD. Dynamic pricing also improved results on all eight domains at eleven milliseconds of planning cost.

arxiv:2611.24181.text: Rare-Tail Statistics For Learning Biased Gaussian Halfspaces with Label Noise. From Arya Mazumdar and colleagues. Learning a Gaussian halfspace becomes difficult when its boundary is far from the center of the data, especially with noisy labels. This work studies a simple estimator that averages only examples from the less common label class. Across several noise models, it recovers the target direction with a near-optimal number of samples, even when labels near the boundary are almost random. It also gives a useful warm start for learning under random label flips, reaching the information-theoretic sample rate up to logarithmic factors.

arxiv:2611.24428.text: Keeping Shielded Data-Driven Controllers Safe Under System Evolution via Model Consistency. From Roland Stolz and colleagues. Data-driven controllers can be hard to trust, and a safety shield may stop working if its assumptions about the physical system become outdated. This work treats the controller, shield, and system as connected models, then checks their consistency as the system changes. When the models no longer agree, automatic rules update them to restore a valid shield. In a reach-avoid task with a unicycle system, this approach maintained safety guarantees as the system changed.

arxiv:2611.23965.text: The S and Double-Exponential Transformations with a Moment Expansion for Three-Centre Coulomb and Hybrid Integrals. From Hassan Safouhi. Three-centre Coulomb and hybrid integrals are difficult to calculate because their radial integrals extend to infinity and oscillate. This work combines a transformation that shifts derivatives away from the oscillating part with a double-exponential quadrature method. The combined approach reaches high accuracy with substantially fewer quadrature points than direct quadrature. For weakly oscillating cases, a convergent moment expansion improves reliability, and tests include complete molecular integrals for water and ethylene.

arxiv:2611.24591.text: Reliable arithmetic circuits using less reliable (sub-digital) logic. From Trevor McCourt and colleagues. Static failures in conventional computer logic are often seen as a hard limit on how far operating voltage can be lowered. This work develops a statistical rule linking the failure rate of individual gates to that of a whole circuit. It shows that circuit failure requires a whole cluster of gates to fail together, and that the needed cluster grows as voltage falls. This suggests that low-voltage logic may be more resilient than expected, and could help reduce the energy demands of artificial intelligence.
